claims.evidence: Inferred from the analysis of cell tracking data.

claims.claim: A marked anterior and ventral departure of brain cells occurs in control embryos from 24 to 26 hpf, representing the onset of the flexure movement.
claims.source: From 24 to 26 hpf we observed a marked anterior and ventral departure of brain cells in control embryos, representing the onset of the flexure movement.
claims.evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4J.

claims.claim: OP cells move anteriorly and ventrally from 24-26 hpf in coordination with the brain, revealing that the OPs are subjected to the flexure movement.
claims.source: Strikingly, OP cells also moved anteriorly and ventrally from these stages, in coordination with the brain, revealing that the OPs are also subjected to the flexure movement (Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1M, Figure 4—video 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1M, and Figure 4—video 1.

claims.claim: The flexure movements are visible in the brain and OPs of sly mutants.
claims.source: The flexure movements were also visible in the brain and OPs of sly mutants (Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1N, Figure 4—video 1), with OP cells moving with a higher MSD than in controls (Figure 4M).
claims.evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1N, and Figure 4—video 1.

claims.claim: OP cells in sly mutants move with a higher MSD than in controls during the forebrain flexure.
claims.source: The flexure movements were also visible in the brain and OPs of sly mutants (Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1N, Figure 4—video 1), with OP cells moving with a higher MSD than in controls (Figure 4M).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4M.

claims.claim: A similar trend of higher MSD is observed for brain cells in sly mutants during the forebrain flexure, but is not statistically significant.
claims.source: A similar trend was observed for brain cells, but was not statistically significant (Figure 4N).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4N.

claims.claim: In 4/4 sly mutant embryos, brain and OP cells exhibit curved trajectories, moving first anteriorly and ventrally, then turning posteriorly.
claims.source: Moreover, upon visualisation of the cell trajectories in a lateral (YZ) view, we noticed that in 4/4 mutant embryos, brain and OP cells exhibited curved trajectories, moving first anteriorly and ventrally, then turning posteriorly, while this phenomenon occurred in only 1/4 control sibling during the duration of our movies (Figure 4—figure supplement 1M, N).
claims.evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1M, N.

claims.claim: Brain and OP cells are subjected to an accelerated or enhanced forebrain flexure remodelling in sly mutants.
claims.source: This reinforces the idea that brain and OP cells are subjected to an accelerated or enhanced forebrain flexure remodelling in the sly mutants, and suggests that in the wild type situation the BMs allow the tissues, and in particular the OP, to resist to the morphogenetic movements associated with the flexure.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation of curved trajectories and higher MSD in mutants.

claims.claim: In the wild type situation, the BMs allow the tissues, particularly the OP, to resist the morphogenetic movements associated with the flexure.
claims.source: This reinforces the idea that brain and OP cells are subjected to an accelerated or enhanced forebrain flexure remodelling in the sly mutants, and suggests that in the wild type situation the BMs allow the tissues, and in particular the OP, to resist to the morphogenetic movements associated with the flexure.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the comparison of cell behaviors in mutants and controls.

claims.claim: The Laminin γ1-containing BMs are required to prevent OP cell scattering during the forebrain flexure.
claims.source: Altogether, our findings show that the Laminin γ1-containing BMs are required to prevent OP cell scattering, maintain OP shape and dampen OP cell movements during the forebrain flexure.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation of ectopic cells and altered OP shape in mutants.

claims.claim: The Laminin γ1-containing BMs are required to maintain OP shape during the forebrain flexure.
claims.source: Altogether, our findings show that the Laminin γ1-containing BMs are required to prevent OP cell scattering, maintain OP shape and dampen OP cell movements during the forebrain flexure.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation of increased DV dimension in mutants.

claims.claim: The Laminin γ1-containing BMs are required to dampen OP cell movements during the forebrain flexure.
claims.source: Altogether, our findings show that the Laminin γ1-containing BMs are required to prevent OP cell scattering, maintain OP shape and dampen OP cell movements during the forebrain flexure.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation of higher MSD in mutants.

claims.claim: In control siblings, OP cells display a lateral displacement during the forebrain flexure.
claims.source: We noticed that, while in control siblings OP cells also display a lateral displacement, they rather move in the medial direction in sly mutants, towards the brain, as if the two OPs were progressively converging towards each other (Figure 4J, L and O).
claims.evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4J and O.

claims.claim: In sly mutants, OP cells move in the medial direction towards the brain during the forebrain flexure.
claims.source: We noticed that, while in control siblings OP cells also display a lateral displacement, they rather move in the medial direction in sly mutants, towards the brain, as if the two OPs were progressively converging towards each other (Figure 4J, L and O).
claims.evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 4L and O.

claims.claim: The two OPs progressively converge towards each other in sly mutants during the forebrain flexure.
claims.source: We noticed that, while in control siblings OP cells also display a lateral displacement, they rather move in the medial direction in sly mutants, towards the brain, as if the two OPs were progressively converging towards each other (Figure 4J, L and O).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation of medial OP cell movement in mutants.

claims.claim: OPs in sly mutants are partially embedded within the brain tissue.
claims.source: Qualitative observations of these z-stacks revealed that OPs in sly mutants are partially embedded within the brain tissue and display a curved and irregular boundary with the brain, while the frontier between the two tissues appears as a straight line in control siblings (Figure 5A, A', Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, A', and Figure 5—video 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A, A', Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, A', and Figure 5—video 1.

claims.claim: OPs in sly mutants display a curved and irregular boundary with the brain.
claims.source: Qualitative observations of these z-stacks revealed that OPs in sly mutants are partially embedded within the brain tissue and display a curved and irregular boundary with the brain, while the frontier between the two tissues appears as a straight line in control siblings (Figure 5A, A', Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, A', and Figure 5—video 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A, A', Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, A', and Figure 5—video 1.

claims.claim: The frontier between the OP and brain appears as a straight line in control siblings.
claims.source: Qualitative observations of these z-stacks revealed that OPs in sly mutants are partially embedded within the brain tissue and display a curved and irregular boundary with the brain, while the frontier between the two tissues appears as a straight line in control siblings (Figure 5A, A', Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, A', and Figure 5—video 1).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A, A', Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, A', and Figure 5—video 1.

claims.claim: The width of the forebrain in sly mutants is smaller than in controls, particularly in anterior and dorsal areas.
claims.source: The width of the forebrain in sly mutants was smaller than in controls, in particular in anterior and dorsal areas (Figure 5B-D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-D).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5B-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-D.

claims.claim: Proliferation is unchanged in the brain of sly mutants.
claims.source: Proliferation was unchanged in the brain of sly mutants, while apoptosis was only sligtly increased (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–L), suggesting that the smaller brain width is due to a local distortion of the tissue rather than a decreased number of cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-L.

claims.claim: Apoptosis is only slightly increased in the brain of sly mutants.
claims.source: Proliferation was unchanged in the brain of sly mutants, while apoptosis was only sligtly increased (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–L), suggesting that the smaller brain width is due to a local distortion of the tissue rather than a decreased number of cells.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-L.

claims.claim: The smaller brain width in sly mutants is due to a local distortion of the tissue rather than a decreased number of cells.
claims.source: Proliferation was unchanged in the brain of sly mutants, while apoptosis was only sligtly increased (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E–L), suggesting that the smaller brain width is due to a local distortion of the tissue rather than a decreased number of cells.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that proliferation is unchanged and apoptosis is only slightly increased.

claims.claim: The OP/brain boundary is less straight in sly mutants compared to controls at 36 hpf.
claims.source: This analysis demonstrated that the OP/brain boundary is less straight in sly mutants as compared with controls (Figure 5G and H).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 5G and H.

claims.claim: The forebrain is smaller and distorted in sly mutants, possibly due to the inward convergence of the two OPs.
claims.source: Thus, our analyses of cell tracks, brain size and proliferation/apoptosis, and of the shape of the brain/OP boundary suggest that the forebrain is smaller and distorted in sly mutants, possibly due to the inward convergence of the two OPs.
claims.evidence: Inferred from multiple observations including cell tracks, brain size, and boundary shape.

claims.claim: The brain may fail to form in the normal size and shape in sly mutants.
claims.source: A non-mutually alternative hypothesis is that the brain fails to form in the normal size and shape in sly mutants.
claims.evidence: Speculative alternative hypothesis.

claims.claim: The Laminin γ1-dependent BMs serve to establish a straight brain/OP boundary preventing local intermixing and late convergence of the two OPs.
claims.source: These findings suggest that the Laminin γ1-dependent BMs serve to establish a straight brain/OP boundary preventing local intermixing and the late convergence of the two OPs towards each other during the flexure movement.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation of irregular boundary and OP convergence in mutants.

claims.claim: Retrograde axon extension appears not to be affected in sly mutants for at least some of the neurog1:GFP+ neurons/axons.
claims.source: Several instances of retrograde extension were seen both in controls and mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B), indicating that retrograde axon extension occurs normally for at least some of the neurog1:GFP+ neurons/axons in sly mutants.
claims.evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B.

claims.claim: Retrograde axon extension occurs normally for at least some of the YFP+ OP neurons in sly mutants.
claims.source: In addition, on fixed Tg(omp:meYFP) sly mutants at 24 hpf, numerous YFP+ neurons had their proximal axonal portion formed and attached to the brain surface (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C–F), suggesting that retrograde axon extension also occurs normally for at least some of the YFP+ OP neurons.
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-F.

claims.claim: The presence of a BM around the OP and/or the brain is not an absolute requirement for the attachment of axon tips to the ventro-medial wall of the OP during retrograde extension.
claims.source: Although we cannot rule out that retrograde axon extension is affected in a subset of OP neurons, for instance in ectopic cells, the presence of a BM around the OP and/or the brain appears not to be an absolute requirement for the attachment of axon tips to the ventro-medial wall of the OP during retrograde extension.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that retrograde extension occurs in mutants lacking BMs.

claims.claim: In sly mutant embryos, most YFP+ axonal protrusions are unable to leave the OP and appear to stall at the OP/brain boundary.
claims.source: In mutant embryos, severe axonal defects were observed. Most YFP+ axonal protrusions were unable to leave the OP and appeared to stall at the OP/brain boundary, leading in some embryos to an apparent absence of axon bundle (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, left column and Figure 4—video 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining and live imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and Figure 4—video 2.

claims.claim: In some sly mutant embryos (8-10%), a small proportion of axons manage to form a bundle reaching the presumptive OB region by ectopically exiting the OP dorsally.
claims.source: In some embryos (8–10%), a small proportion of axons managed form a bundle reaching the presumptive OB region by ectopically exiting the OP dorsally (an exit point location never observed in the control fish), while the axons would normally exit the OP at a more ventro-medial position in the controls (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, left column and Figure 4—video 2).
claims.evidence: Supported by immunostaining and live imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G and Figure 4—video 2.

claims.claim: An increased proportion of embryos with ectopic medial projections is observed in sly mutants (18-30% depending on the stage, compared to 0-9% in controls).
claims.source: In addition, an increased proportion of embryos with ectopic medial projections was observed in mutants (18–30% of the embryos depending on the stage, as compared to 0 to 9% in controls, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, right column).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: There is a tendency for a higher percentage of embryos displaying ventral projections in sly mutants, particularly visible at 24 hpf.
claims.source: Finally, there is a tendency for a higher percentage of embryos displaying ventral projections in the sly mutant, particularly visible at 24 hpf (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G, middle column).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Growth cones in sly mutants do not display a directional migration towards the bulb during the whole movie duration.
claims.source: By contrast, growth cones in the sly mutants did not display a directional migration towards the bulb, during the whole movie duration (Figure 6C, F1 and L).
claims.evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 6C, F1 and L.

claims.claim: Growth cones in sly mutants are motile and explore the environment, but move on short distances and/or without preferential direction, resulting in perturbed axon growth.
claims.source: They were motile and explored the environment, as shown by speed and persistence measurements, but moved on short distances and/or without preferential direction, resulting in a perturbed axon growth (Figure 6C–N).
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6C-N.

claims.claim: The migration of the olfactory axons is impaired in sly mutants.
claims.source: These live imaging analyses confirm that the migration of the olfactory axons is impaired in sly mutants.
claims.evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of growth cone behavior.

claims.claim: Laminin γ1-dependent BMs are essential for the growth and navigation of the axons from the OP to the olfactory bulb.
claims.source: Altogether, our results show that Laminin γ1-dependent BMs are essential for the growth and navigation of the axons from the OP to the olfactory bulb.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation of severe axonal defects in mutants.

claims.claim: Crestin-labelled NCC are absent from the brain/OP interface in sly mutants at 32 hpf.
claims.source: In situ hybridisation for the NCC marker crestin (Luo et al., 2001) revealed that, while a clear NCC cluster can be seen at the brain/OP interface in controls at 32 hpf, crestin-labelled NCC are absent from this area in sly mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, A').
claims.evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, A'.

claims.claim: Laminin γ1-dependent BMs are important for NCC migration or survival in the brain/OP interface region.
claims.source: This suggests that Laminin γ1-dependent BMs are important for NCC migration or survival in this region of the embryo.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the absence of NCC at the brain/OP interface in mutants.

claims.claim: In sly mutants, numerous motile NCC are observed close to the OP at 16 hpf in all analyzed placodes (8/8).
claims.source: Surprisingly, in sly mutants, numerous motile NCC were also observed close to the OP at 16 hpf in all the analysed placodes (8/8), and populated the eye/OP interface in 7/8 placodes (10/10 in controls; Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: In sly mutants, NCC populate the eye/OP interface in 7/8 placodes.
claims.source: Surprisingly, in sly mutants, numerous motile NCC were also observed close to the OP at 16 hpf in all the analysed placodes (8/8), and populated the eye/OP interface in 7/8 placodes (10/10 in controls; Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: In sly mutants, NCC are observed in the dorsal region of the brain/OP boundary in only 2/8 placodes.
claims.source: By contrast, in sly mutants, NCC were observed in the dorsal region of the brain/OP boundary in only 2/8 placodes, and in the ventral brain/OP frontier in only 2/8 placodes as well.
claims.evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: In sly mutants, NCC are observed in the ventral brain/OP frontier in only 2/8 placodes.
claims.source: By contrast, in sly mutants, NCC were observed in the dorsal region of the brain/OP boundary in only 2/8 placodes, and in the ventral brain/OP frontier in only 2/8 placodes as well.
claims.evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: In sly mutants, NCC that initially populated the ventral brain/OP interface are expelled from the boundary at later stages.
claims.source: Interestingly, in these two samples, NCC that had initially populated the ventral brain/OP interface were then expelled from the boundary at later stages (Figure 5—video 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: Supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 5—video 2 and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: The migration of cranial NCC towards the OP and between the eye and OP is only partially impaired in sly mutants.
claims.source: Altogether, these live imaging data suggest that the migration of cranial NCC towards the OP and between the eye and OP is only partially impaired in sly mutants.
claims.evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of NCC migration.

claims.claim: The subset of NCC that populate the OP/forebrain appears to be more specifically affected in sly mutants, with defects in their migration to the interface and/or the maintenance of their position at the interface.
claims.source: The subset of NCC that populate the OP/forebrain appears to be more specifically affected, with defects in their migration to the interface and/or the maintenance of their position at the interface.
claims.evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of NCC behavior at the OP/forebrain interface.

claims.claim: No significant difference is observed between controls and foxd3 -/- mutants for OP dimensions and axon bundle length at 28 and 36 hpf.
claims.source: No significant difference was observed between controls and foxd3 -/- mutants for these parameters (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C–L), suggesting that the late OP morphogenesis and axonal phenotypes of the sly mutants are not a consequence of the impairment of NCC development.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3C-L.

claims.claim: The late OP morphogenesis and axonal phenotypes of the sly mutants are not a consequence of the impairment of NCC development.
claims.source: No significant difference was observed between controls and foxd3 -/- mutants for these parameters (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C–L), suggesting that the late OP morphogenesis and axonal phenotypes of the sly mutants are not a consequence of the impairment of NCC development.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the comparison of sly and foxd3 mutant phenotypes.

claims.claim: The BM of the OP prevents its deformation in response to the mechanical forces generated by the morphogenetic movement of the neighbouring brain.
claims.source: We thus propose that the BM of the OP prevents its deformation in response to the mechanical forces generated by the morphogenetic movement of the neighbouring brain.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that the OP deforms in mutants lacking BMs during the flexure.

claims.claim: The ability of the placode's BM to limit the deformation of the OP during the flexure most probably relies on its stiffness.
claims.source: The ability of the placode's BM to limit the deformation of the OP during this developmental step most probably relies on its stiffness.
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation based on known mechanical properties of BMs.

claims.claim: In the Drosophila egg chamber, Collagen IV has a major contribution to BM mechanical properties, particularly to its stiffness.
claims.source: In the Drosophila egg chamber, while Laminin itself has a minor contribution to the BM mechanical properties, Collagen IV, which deposition in the BM depends on Laminin (Díaz de la Loza et al., 2017) has a major contribution to these properties, and in particular to its stiffness (Töpfer et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The putative loss of mechanical properties leading to OP deformation in the sly mutant may be due to Collagen IV rather than Laminin itself.
claims.source: Even though the putative loss of mechanical properties leading to OP deformation observed in the sly mutant is a consequence of a Laminin loss-of-function, it remains conceivable that it is the Collagen IV, rather than the Laminin itself, which is responsible of these mechanical properties in wild-type animals.
claims.evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on the role of Collagen IV in other systems.

claims.claim: A dramatic consequence of the absence of proper OP and brain BMs in the sly mutant is the irregular and undefined frontier between the brain and OP.
claims.source: A dramatic consequence of the absence of proper OP and brain BMs in the sly mutant is the irregular and undefined frontier between the brain and OP, with placodal cells tending to locally intermingle with brain cells, and vice versa, along the OP/brain interface.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observations of the brain/OP boundary in mutants.

claims.claim: Tissue intermixing has been observed in the pharynx of Laminin mutants in C. elegans.
claims.source: Tissue intermixing has also been observed in the pharynx of Laminin mutants in C. elegans (Huang et al., 2003) and in the Xenopus notochord upon loss-of-function of the Dystroglycan, a major Laminin receptor (Buisson et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Tissue intermixing has been observed in the Xenopus notochord upon loss-of-function of Dystroglycan, a major Laminin receptor.
claims.source: Tissue intermixing has also been observed in the pharynx of Laminin mutants in C. elegans (Huang et al., 2003) and in the Xenopus notochord upon loss-of-function of the Dystroglycan, a major Laminin receptor (Buisson et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The absence of a clear boundary between the OP and the brain in the sly mutant is accompanied by an apparent distortion of the brain, with notably reduced dimension in its medio-lateral axis.
claims.source: The absence of a clear boundary between the OP and the brain in the sly mutant is accompanied by an apparent distortion of the brain, with notable reduced dimension in its medio-lateral axis.
claims.evidence: Inferred from measurements of brain width in mutants.

claims.claim: The brain distortion in sly mutants is possibly due to the inward migration of the placodes that become partially embedded in the brain.
claims.source: This phenotype, possibly due to the inward migration of the placodes that become partially embedded in the brain, illustrates an additional and unexpected role of the OP and brain BMs, in preventing late convergence of the two placodes towards each other during the flexure movement.
claims.evidence: Speculative interpretation of the brain distortion phenotype.

claims.claim: The OP and brain BMs play a role in preventing late convergence of the two placodes towards each other during the flexure movement.
claims.source: This phenotype, possibly due to the inward migration of the placodes that become partially embedded in the brain, illustrates an additional and unexpected role of the OP and brain BMs, in preventing late convergence of the two placodes towards each other during the flexure movement.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation of OP convergence in mutants.

claims.claim: The early development of zebrafish olfactory axons begins with their retrograde extension, involving the attachment of the tips of the axonal protrusions to the brain's surface, followed by a lateral movement of the OP cell bodies in the opposite direction.
claims.source: The early development of zebrafish olfactory axons begins with their retrograde extension, involving the attachment of the tips of the axonal protrusions to the brain's surface, followed by a lateral movement of the OP cell bodies in the opposite direction (Breau et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Laminin-dependent BMs are dispensable for retrograde axon extension in the olfactory system.
claims.source: These results suggest that Laminin-dependent BMs are dispensable for this retrograde axon extension and, more specifically, that Laminin γ1 itself or other components of the BMs are unlikely to play a role in the anchoring of those axon tips onto the brain's surface, which is a prerequisite for their retrograde extension.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that retrograde extension occurs in mutants lacking BMs.

claims.claim: Laminin γ1 or other BM components are unlikely to play a role in the anchoring of axon tips onto the brain's surface during retrograde extension.
claims.source: These results suggest that Laminin-dependent BMs are dispensable for this retrograde axon extension and, more specifically, that Laminin γ1 itself or other components of the BMs are unlikely to play a role in the anchoring of those axon tips onto the brain's surface, which is a prerequisite for their retrograde extension.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that retrograde extension occurs in mutants lacking BMs.

claims.claim: Following retrograde elongation in the OP, the axons grow and navigate using bona fide growth cones.
claims.source: Our study shows that following retrograde elongation in the OP, the axons grow and navigate using bona fide growth cones, assemble a tight axon fascicle which crosses the BM of the OP, turns and migrates dorsally for a short distance between both BMs and thereafter crosses the brain BM to navigate towards the olfactory bulb.
claims.evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of axon behavior.

claims.claim: The olfactory axons assemble a tight axon fascicle which crosses the BM of the OP.
claims.source: Our study shows that following retrograde elongation in the OP, the axons grow and navigate using bona fide growth cones, assemble a tight axon fascicle which crosses the BM of the OP, turns and migrates dorsally for a short distance between both BMs and thereafter crosses the brain BM to navigate towards the olfactory bulb.
claims.evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of axon behavior.

claims.claim: The olfactory axons turn and migrate dorsally for a short distance between both BMs.
claims.source: Our study shows that following retrograde elongation in the OP, the axons grow and navigate using bona fide growth cones, assemble a tight axon fascicle which crosses the BM of the OP, turns and migrates dorsally for a short distance between both BMs and thereafter crosses the brain BM to navigate towards the olfactory bulb.
claims.evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of axon behavior.

claims.claim: The olfactory axons cross the brain BM to navigate towards the olfactory bulb.
claims.source: Our study shows that following retrograde elongation in the OP, the axons grow and navigate using bona fide growth cones, assemble a tight axon fascicle which crosses the BM of the OP, turns and migrates dorsally for a short distance between both BMs and thereafter crosses the brain BM to navigate towards the olfactory bulb.
claims.evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of axon behavior.

claims.claim: The olfactory axons have to cross two BMs during their development.
claims.source: In other words, the olfactory axons have to cross two BMs.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the description of axon behavior.

claims.claim: The axons cross the first BM as it is still under construction and contains perforations, taking advantage of BM-free small pores to exit the OP.
claims.source: Our data show that the axons cross the first BM as it is still under construction and contains perforations, thus taking advantage of BM-free small pores to exit the OP and reach the narrow area located between the two BMs.
claims.evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations of BM assembly and axon exit.

claims.claim: The axons may locally degrade the BM through the secretion of matrix metalloproteases to enter the brain.
claims.source: It will be interesting, in future work, to determine whether the axons locally degrade the BM through the secretion of matrix metalloproteases, or displace the BM with protrusive forces, or use a combination of both mechanisms (Chang and Chaudhuri, 2019; Ihara et al., 2011; Nazari et al., 2022; Yamada et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Speculative hypothesis for future investigation, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The axons may displace the BM with protrusive forces to enter the brain.
claims.source: It will be interesting, in future work, to determine whether the axons locally degrade the BM through the secretion of matrix metalloproteases, or displace the BM with protrusive forces, or use a combination of both mechanisms (Chang and Chaudhuri, 2019; Ihara et al., 2011; Nazari et al., 2022; Yamada et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: Speculative hypothesis for future investigation, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Olfactory axons remain confined in close proximity to the Laminin-rich BMs as they migrate in the narrow corridor between the OP and brain BMs.
claims.source: As they migrate in the narrow corridor between the OP and brain BMs, olfactory axons remain confined in close proximity to the Laminin-rich BMs.
claims.evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations.

claims.claim: Once in the brain tissue, the distalmost tip of the olfactory axon bundle grows in close apposition to the internal surface of the brain's BM.
claims.source: Importantly, once they have reached the brain tissue, the distalmost tip of this axon bundle still grows in close apposition to the internal surface of the brain's BM, suggesting that this BM serves as a migratory path promoting the growth of these axons.
claims.evidence: Inferred from live imaging observations.

claims.claim: The brain's BM serves as a migratory path promoting the growth of olfactory axons.
claims.source: Importantly, once they have reached the brain tissue, the distalmost tip of this axon bundle still grows in close apposition to the internal surface of the brain's BM, suggesting that this BM serves as a migratory path promoting the growth of these axons.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that axon tips grow along the BM.

claims.claim: The axon growth and directionality phenotype in sly mutants is unlikely to be the result of defects in neuronal differentiation.
claims.source: This phenotype is unlikely to be the result of defects in neuronal differentiation, as demonstrated by HuC immunolabelling and expression of the Tg(neurog1:GFP) and Tg(omp:meYFP) transgenes, which do not show obvious difference as compared to control animals, but appears to be rather due to axon growth and navigation defects.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that neuronal markers are expressed normally in mutants.

claims.claim: The axon phenotype in sly mutants appears to be due to axon growth and navigation defects.
claims.source: This phenotype is unlikely to be the result of defects in neuronal differentiation, as demonstrated by HuC immunolabelling and expression of the Tg(neurog1:GFP) and Tg(omp:meYFP) transgenes, which do not show obvious difference as compared to control animals, but appears to be rather due to axon growth and navigation defects.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation of impaired axon migration in mutants.

claims.claim: Laminin is a good candidate for acting as a privileged substrate for olfactory axons.
claims.source: We did not formally identify the component(s) of the BM involved in this axon extension and pathfinding, but we consider Laminin itself as a good candidate for acting as a privileged substrate the axons, as Laminin does so for other populations of axons in zebrafish (Paulus and Halloran, 2006; Semina et al., 2006), and has been shown in rodents to favor OSN axon extension in vitro, and to be present in vivo along the path followed by OSN axons from the olfactory epithelium to the bulb (Kafitz and Greer, 1997).
claims.evidence: Speculative hypothesis supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Laminin accelerates the growth of axons through binding to integrins, which favors the formation of F-actin in the growth cone in a microtubule- and Rac1-dependent manner.
claims.source: From a molecular point of view, it has been established on cultured sympathetic neurons that Laminin accelerates the growth of axons through binding to integrins, which favors the formation of F-actin in the growth cone in a microtubule- and Rac1-dependent manner (Grabham et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Laminin promotes hippocampal neuron growth cone enhanced progression on stiff substrate through its interaction with L1, highlighting a mechanosensitive axon outgrowth mediated by a L1-Laminin clutch mechanism.
claims.source: Recently, Abe et al., 2021 further documented another role of Laminin in promoting hippocampal neuron growth cones enhanced progression on stiff substrate, through its interaction with L1, highlighting a new mechanosensitive axon outgrowth mediated by a L1-Laminin clutch mechanism (Abe et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Other components of the BM, also affected in the sly mutant, may be involved in the regulation of olfactory axon development.
claims.source: Other components of the BM, also affected in the sly mutant, may be involved as well in the regulation of olfactory axon development.
claims.evidence: Speculative hypothesis.

claims.claim: In rodents, the characterization of ECM protein expression along the developing olfactory pathway revealed a complex interplay between ECM permissive and inhibitory cues expressed dynamically, appearing to restrict axons to the pathway while promoting axon outgrowth within.
claims.source: Still in rodents indeed, the characterisation of the expression of ECM proteins along the developing olfactory pathway unraveled a complex interplay between ECM permissive and inhibitory cues expressed in a dynamic way, appearing to restrict axons to the pathway while promoting axon outgrowth within (Shay et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Guidance cues interacting with BM molecules may be involved in some aspects of the axonal defects observed in the sly mutant.
claims.source: In addition to ECM molecules present in the BMs, guidance cues interacting with these molecules may also be involved in some aspects of the axonal defects observed in the sly mutant.
claims.evidence: Speculative hypothesis.

claims.claim: Xenopus retinal axons are repulsed by ephrin-A5 on fibronectin but attracted by ephrin-A5 on Laminin.
claims.source: For example, while Xenopus retinal axons are repulsed by ephrin-A5 on fibronectin, they are attracted by ephrin-A5 on Laminin (Weinl et al., 2003), and Laminin converts netrin-mediated attraction of these axons to repulsion (Höpker et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Laminin converts netrin-mediated attraction of Xenopus retinal axons to repulsion.
claims.source: For example, while Xenopus retinal axons are repulsed by ephrin-A5 on fibronectin, they are attracted by ephrin-A5 on Laminin (Weinl et al., 2003), and Laminin converts netrin-mediated attraction of these axons to repulsion (Höpker et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The repulsive effect of slit2 on Robo expressing axons of dorsal root ganglia neurons is lost in absence of Laminin.
claims.source: Moreover, whereas slit2 repulses Robo expressing axons of dorsal root ganglia neurons, this repulsive effect is lost in absence of Laminin (Nguyen-Ba-Charvet et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Netrin1a and 1b are expressed in the zebrafish forebrain close to the route of the olfactory axons, where they play an attractive role for olfactory axons which express the netrin receptor DCC.
claims.source: Netrin1a and 1b are expressed in the zebrafish forebrain close to the route of the axons, where they play an attractive role for olfactory axons which express the netrin receptor DCC (Dang et al., 2023; Lakhina et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Several ephrin and slits ligands are expressed in the forebrain at stages of axonal growth.
claims.source: In addition, several ephrin and slits ligands are expressed in the forebrain at stages of axonal growth (https://zfin.org/, Miyasaka et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to database and previous literature.

claims.claim: The absence of Laminin in the sly mutant may change the netrin-, ephrin- or slit-dependent pathfinding of olfactory axons.
claims.source: We may thus envisage that the absence of Laminin in the sly mutant may change in some way the netrin-, ephrin- or slit-dependent pathfinding of olfactory axons.
claims.evidence: Speculative hypothesis based on known interactions between Laminin and guidance cues.

claims.claim: The boundary between the sensory and central components of the olfactory system is organised by the BMs of the OP and the brain.
claims.source: In conclusion, our findings indicate that the boundary between the sensory and central components of the olfactory system (Suter and Jaworski, 2019) is organised by the BMs of the OP and the brain.
claims.evidence: Inferred from multiple observations of BM function in organizing the OP/brain boundary.

claims.claim: The BMs of the OP and brain are permeable at specific locations to allow the sensory axons to enter the brain and use them as a substrate to grow towards the olfactory bulb.
claims.source: These BMs are permeable at specific locations to allow the sensory axons to enter the brain and use them as a substrate to grow towards the olfactory bulb, and at the same time they maintain OP shape and position in the face of major morphogenetic movements occuring during the brain flexure, and ensure proper separation of the two tissues by preventing their intermixing.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observations of BM interruptions at exit/entry points and axon-BM interactions.

claims.claim: The BMs of the OP and brain maintain OP shape and position in the face of major morphogenetic movements occurring during the brain flexure.
claims.source: These BMs are permeable at specific locations to allow the sensory axons to enter the brain and use them as a substrate to grow towards the olfactory bulb, and at the same time they maintain OP shape and position in the face of major morphogenetic movements occuring during the brain flexure, and ensure proper separation of the two tissues by preventing their intermixing.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observations of OP deformation and displacement in mutants lacking BMs.

claims.claim: The BMs of the OP and brain ensure proper separation of the two tissues by preventing their intermixing.
claims.source: These BMs are permeable at specific locations to allow the sensory axons to enter the brain and use them as a substrate to grow towards the olfactory bulb, and at the same time they maintain OP shape and position in the face of major morphogenetic movements occuring during the brain flexure, and ensure proper separation of the two tissues by preventing their intermixing.
claims.evidence: Inferred from observations of tissue intermixing in mutants lacking BMs.

results.result: Laminin-rich basement membranes (BMs) assemble around the brain and olfactory placode (OP) during zebrafish development. A fairly continuous Laminin-rich BM surrounds the brain from 17-18 hpf, while only discrete Laminin spots are detected around the OP at this stage. By 22 hpf, two distinct BMs are visible—one around the brain and another partially enveloping the OP on its basal side—suggesting that the OP's Laminin-rich BM assembles between 18 and 22 hpf during late OP coalescence.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are well-supported by immunostaining data (Figure 1A-B') and consistent with cited previous studies. The temporal progression from discrete spots to continuous BM is clearly documented, and the inference about BM assembly timing (C4) logically follows from the observations at 18 and 22 hpf.

results.result: Live imaging reveals the cellular sources of Laminin γ1 deposition during OP development. Mesenchymal cells (likely neural crest cells and/or periocular mesenchyme), a subset of OP cells, and telencephalic cells all exhibit cytoplasmic Laminin-sfGFP expression. These observations suggest that Laminin γ1 around the OP is deposited during late coalescence stages from multiple cellular sources, while the forebrain contributes to its own BM deposition.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C10 are supported by live imaging data using the TgBAC(lamC1:lamC1-sfGFP) reporter line (Figure 1—videos 1-2). The identification of multiple cellular sources is well-documented, though the identity of mesenchymal cells (C6) remains tentative based on literature citations. The inferences about timing and cellular contributions (C8, C10) are reasonable given the imaging evidence.

results.result: BMs around the brain and OP contain specific interruptions at axon exit and entry points. At 28-36 hpf, continuous BM-like signals envelop both tissues except where olfactory axons exit the OP and enter the brain. Live imaging reveals that the exit point forms through incomplete BM synthesis rather than perforation of pre-existing BM, while the entry point opens concomitantly with axon arrival. Axons initially grow dorsally between the two BMs, then their distal tips migrate along the internal surface of the brain's BM, suggesting BMs serve as migratory paths.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C23 are well-supported by both fixed immunostaining (Figure 1C-D') and live imaging data (Figure 1—videos 2-4). The temporal sequence of BM interruption formation is clearly documented. However, C24 is speculative and represents a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated result. The mechanism of entry point opening (C20) is inferred but not directly tested.

results.result: The sly mutant shows complete loss of Laminin BM-like accumulation and disrupted BM integrity. Laminin cannot be detected in sly -/- mutants from 16-36 hpf, while heterozygous embryos appear normal. Nidogen BM staining is also absent in mutants. Collagen IV pattern is dramatically disrupted but not completely abolished, with discrete fibrous patches remaining around the OP instead of the linear BM-like staining seen in controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C32 are strongly supported by immunostaining data (Figure 2A-I') and consistent with cited previous studies on the sly mutant. The differential effects on Nidogen (complete loss) versus Collagen IV (disrupted but not abolished) are clearly documented. The inference about absence of maternal Laminin (C27) is reasonable given detection limits from 16 hpf onwards.

results.result: Electron microscopy reveals severely compromised BM ultrastructure in sly mutants. In controls at 24 hpf, a 120 nm-wide gap containing electron-dense ECM material (likely representing BMs) separates neural crest cells from adjacent OP and brain cells. In sly mutants, almost no neural crest cells are detected, and the gap between OP and brain cells is significantly reduced to 40 nm and mostly devoid of electron-dense material. Similar defects persist at 32 hpf, while intercellular gaps within the OP or brain tissues are unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C41 are well-supported by quantitative electron microscopy data (Figure 2J-N, Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The measurements show statistically significant differences in gap thickness at the brain/OP interface. The identification of BM material (C34) and inference about NCC development (C36) are reasonable but somewhat speculative. The conclusion about BM integrity (C41) is strongly supported and consistent with literature.

results.result: OP coalescence proceeds relatively normally in sly mutants despite BM loss. At 22 hpf, the mediolateral dimension of OP cell clusters is increased in mutants, but AP and DV dimensions are unchanged. This is not due to altered proliferation or apoptosis. Live cell tracking reveals no significant difference in OP cell mean square displacement (MSD) or ML/DV displacement, though brain cell MSD is higher in mutants. Non-significant trends suggest anterior shifts in final OP cell positions. Overall, OP cells condense into compact clusters with normal movement parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C53 are supported by quantitative morphometric data (Figure 3A-E) and live cell tracking analysis (Figure 3F-P). The statistical analyses are appropriate, though some trends (C50-C51) lack significance. The conclusion (C53) appropriately acknowledges that while brain cell movements are affected, OP coalescence proceeds relatively normally. The speculative claim C52 is appropriately tentative.

results.result: Laminin γ1-containing BMs are required to maintain OP shape and dampen cell movements during forebrain flexure. From 24-26 hpf, both brain and OP cells move anteriorly and ventrally, revealing that OPs are subjected to flexure movements. In sly mutants, flexure movements are visible but OP cells move with higher MSD than controls, and cells exhibit curved trajectories. These findings indicate that BMs prevent OP cell scattering, maintain OP shape, and dampen OP cell movements during the flexure, allowing tissues to resist morphogenetic forces.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C64 are well-supported by live imaging and cell tracking data (Figure 4I-O, Figure 4—videos 1). The discovery that OPs undergo flexure movements (C55) is novel and well-documented. The increased MSD in mutants (C57) is statistically significant. The curved trajectories (C59) are observed in 4/4 mutants vs 1/4 controls. The inferences about BM function (C60-C64) are reasonable given the comparative data, though causality is inferred rather than directly tested.

results.result: Laminin γ1-dependent BMs establish a straight brain/OP boundary and prevent OP convergence. In controls, OP cells display lateral displacement during flexure, while in sly mutants they move medially toward the brain, causing OP convergence. Mutant OPs are partially embedded in brain tissue with curved, irregular boundaries, while controls show straight boundaries. The forebrain width is reduced in mutants, particularly in anterior and dorsal areas, due to tissue distortion rather than cell loss (proliferation unchanged, apoptosis slightly increased). Quantitative analysis confirms the OP/brain boundary is less straight in mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C78 are supported by multiple complementary approaches: live imaging (Figure 4J-O), 3D immunostaining (Figure 5A-D), and quantitative boundary analysis (Figure 5E-H). The statistical analyses are appropriate and show significant differences. The inference about tissue distortion vs cell loss (C74) is well-supported by proliferation/apoptosis data. The alternative hypothesis (C77) is appropriately presented as speculative. The conclusion about BM function (C78) is reasonable but represents inference rather than direct demonstration.

results.result: Retrograde axon extension appears largely unaffected in sly mutants. Live imaging shows instances of retrograde extension in both controls and mutants for neurog1:GFP+ neurons. Fixed imaging at 24 hpf reveals numerous YFP+ neurons with proximal axonal portions attached to the brain surface in mutants. These observations suggest that BMs around the OP and brain are not absolutely required for axon tip attachment during retrograde extension, though effects on subsets of neurons cannot be ruled out.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 are supported by live imaging (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B) and fixed imaging data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C-F). However, the analysis is qualitative rather than quantitative, and the authors appropriately acknowledge they cannot rule out effects on subsets of neurons. The conclusion (C81) is appropriately cautious, stating BMs are not an 'absolute requirement' rather than claiming no role whatsoever.

results.result: Laminin γ1-dependent BMs are essential for olfactory axon growth and navigation from the OP to the olfactory bulb. In sly mutants, most YFP+ axonal protrusions cannot leave the OP and stall at the OP/brain boundary. A small proportion (8-10%) of embryos show ectopic dorsal exit points. Increased proportions of embryos display ectopic medial projections (18-30% vs 0-9% in controls) and ventral projections. Live imaging reveals that mutant growth cones are motile but do not display directional migration toward the bulb, moving short distances without preferential direction, resulting in impaired axon migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C89 are well-supported by both fixed imaging (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G) and quantitative live imaging of growth cone behavior (Figure 6A-N). The statistical analyses of growth cone trajectories, speed, and persistence are appropriate. The conclusion (C89) is strongly supported by converging evidence from multiple approaches. However, the specific molecular mechanisms remain unidentified.

results.result: Neural crest cell (NCC) development is affected in sly mutants, particularly at the OP/forebrain interface. In situ hybridization shows crestin-labeled NCC are absent from the brain/OP interface in mutants at 32 hpf. However, live imaging reveals that NCC migration toward the OP and between eye and OP is only partially impaired—numerous motile NCC reach the OP vicinity at 16 hpf in all mutant placodes (8/8), and most populate the eye/OP interface (7/8). The subset of NCC at the OP/forebrain interface is more specifically affected, with reduced presence at dorsal (2/8) and ventral (2/8) boundaries, and NCC that initially populate the ventral interface are expelled at later stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C98 are supported by in situ hybridization (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-A') and live imaging data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, Figure 5—video 2). The apparent contradiction between complete absence at 32 hpf (C90) and partial presence at earlier stages (C92-C96) is explained by the specific loss at the OP/forebrain interface. The inferences about migration vs survival (C91) and specific effects on interface populations (C98) are reasonable but not definitively tested.

results.result: The late OP morphogenesis and axonal phenotypes in sly mutants are not consequences of impaired NCC development. Analysis of foxd3 -/- mutants, which show similar NCC defects to sly mutants (loss of crestin at brain/OP interface), reveals no significant differences from controls in OP dimensions or axon bundle length at 28 and 36 hpf. This genetic dissection demonstrates that the OP and axonal phenotypes observed in sly mutants result from direct loss of BM function rather than indirect effects through NCC defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 are supported by quantitative comparison of foxd3 mutants and controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C-L). This is an important control experiment that strengthens the interpretation of the sly mutant phenotypes. The logic is sound: if NCC loss caused the OP/axon phenotypes, foxd3 mutants should show similar defects, but they do not. However, this does not completely rule out that NCC contribute to normal development, only that their loss is not sufficient to cause the observed phenotypes.

results.result: The mechanical properties of BMs, particularly stiffness, likely mediate their role in preventing OP deformation during forebrain flexure. The authors propose that the OP's BM prevents deformation in response to mechanical forces from neighboring brain morphogenetic movements, with this function most probably relying on BM stiffness. Literature from Drosophila egg chamber shows Collagen IV has major contributions to BM stiffness. The authors speculate that Collagen IV, rather than Laminin itself, may be responsible for the mechanical properties in wild-type animals, even though the sly phenotype results from Laminin loss-of-function.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C104 represent reasonable hypotheses based on the observed phenotypes and literature precedent (C103 is well-supported by citations), but they lack direct experimental support in this study. No biomechanical measurements of BM stiffness or mechanical properties were performed. Claims C102 and C104 are explicitly speculative. While the hypothesis is plausible and well-reasoned, it requires future experimental validation through direct mechanical measurements or Collagen IV-specific manipulations.

results.result: Loss of proper BMs in sly mutants causes tissue intermixing and brain distortion. The absence of proper OP and brain BMs results in an irregular, undefined frontier with local intermixing of placodal and brain cells along the interface. This is accompanied by apparent brain distortion with reduced mediolateral dimension. The authors propose this phenotype may result from inward migration of placodes that become partially embedded in the brain, illustrating a role for BMs in preventing late convergence of the two placodes during flexure.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C110 are supported by multiple lines of evidence including 3D imaging (Figure 5A-D), quantitative boundary analysis (Figure 5E-H), and brain width measurements (Figure 5B-D). The tissue intermixing observation (C105) is well-documented and consistent with literature examples in other systems (C106-C107). However, the proposed mechanism (C109) is speculative—the brain distortion could result from OP convergence or from independent brain morphogenesis defects (alternative hypothesis mentioned in text). The causal relationship requires further investigation.

results.result: Laminin-dependent BMs are dispensable for retrograde axon extension and axon tip anchoring. The early development of zebrafish olfactory axons involves retrograde extension with axon tip attachment to the brain surface followed by lateral OP cell body movement. Since retrograde extension occurs in sly mutants lacking BMs, the authors conclude that Laminin-dependent BMs are dispensable for this process, and specifically that Laminin γ1 or other BM components are unlikely to play a role in anchoring axon tips to the brain surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 are supported by the observation that retrograde extension occurs in sly mutants (C79-C80). Claim C111 is well-established by cited literature. The inferences (C112-C113) are reasonable given the mutant data, though the authors appropriately acknowledge they cannot rule out effects on subsets of neurons. The conclusion is appropriately stated as 'dispensable' and 'unlikely to play a role' rather than claiming definitively no role, acknowledging the limitations of the analysis.

results.result: Olfactory axons navigate a complex path involving crossing two BMs during development. Following retrograde elongation, axons grow using bona fide growth cones, assemble into a tight fascicle that crosses the OP's BM, migrate dorsally between both BMs, then cross the brain BM to navigate toward the olfactory bulb. The axons cross the first BM while it is still under construction by taking advantage of BM-free pores, rather than perforating a pre-existing complete BM.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C119 are well-supported by detailed live imaging observations (Figure 1E-J, Figure 1—videos 1-4). The temporal sequence of BM assembly and axon exit is clearly documented. The inference that axons use pre-existing pores rather than perforating the BM (C119) is strongly supported by the observation that BM interruptions are present as the BM assembles (C15-C16). This represents a novel and important finding about the mechanism of axon exit from the OP.

results.result: The mechanism by which axons cross the brain BM to enter remains to be determined. The authors propose that axons may locally degrade the BM through matrix metalloprotease secretion, displace the BM with protrusive forces, or use a combination of both mechanisms. These represent hypotheses for future investigation supported by literature citations.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C121 are explicitly presented as speculative hypotheses for future work. While the observation that the entry point opens concomitantly with axon arrival (C19) suggests axons actively create the opening, the specific mechanism is not tested in this study. The hypotheses are reasonable and supported by literature citations showing these mechanisms operate in other contexts, but they require direct experimental validation.

results.result: The brain's BM serves as a migratory substrate for olfactory axons. As axons migrate in the narrow corridor between OP and brain BMs, they remain confined in close proximity to Laminin-rich BMs. Once in the brain tissue, the distalmost tip of the axon bundle grows in close apposition to the internal surface of the brain's BM, suggesting this BM serves as a migratory path promoting axon growth.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C124 are supported by live imaging observations (Figure 1H-I, Figure 1—videos 2 and 4) showing consistent close apposition of axon tips to the brain's BM. The inference that the BM serves as a migratory path (C124) is strongly supported by the severe axon navigation defects in sly mutants (C82-C89). However, the specific molecular mechanisms and whether this represents active guidance vs passive constraint are not definitively established.

results.result: Axon phenotypes in sly mutants result from growth and navigation defects rather than neuronal differentiation defects. The axon growth and directionality phenotype is unlikely to result from defects in neuronal differentiation, as demonstrated by normal HuC immunolabeling and expression of Tg(neurog1:GFP) and Tg(omp:meYFP) transgenes. Instead, the phenotype appears to be due to axon growth and navigation defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C126 are supported by the observation that neuronal markers are expressed normally in mutants, indicating neurons differentiate properly. This is an important control that strengthens the interpretation that the axonal defects are specific to growth and navigation rather than reflecting general neuronal dysfunction. However, the analysis of neuronal differentiation is relatively superficial—more detailed molecular characterization of neuronal subtypes could strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Multiple ECM and guidance cue mechanisms may contribute to olfactory axon pathfinding. The authors consider Laminin itself a good candidate substrate based on its roles in other zebrafish axon populations and rodent olfactory system. Literature shows Laminin accelerates axon growth through integrin binding and F-actin formation, and promotes mechanosensitive outgrowth via L1-Laminin interactions. Other BM components and guidance cues (netrins, ephrins, slits) that interact with Laminin may also be involved. The absence of Laminin in sly mutants may alter the function of these guidance cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C138 represent a comprehensive discussion of potential mechanisms supported by extensive literature citations (C128-C129, C131, C133-C137). However, these are largely speculative hypotheses (C127, C130, C132, C138) that were not directly tested in this study. The specific molecular components of the BM involved in axon guidance were not formally identified (acknowledged in C127). While the hypotheses are well-reasoned and grounded in literature, they require future experimental validation through specific molecular manipulations.

results.result: BMs of the OP and brain organize the boundary between sensory and central components of the olfactory system with multiple functions. The BMs are permeable at specific locations to allow sensory axons to enter the brain and use them as substrates for growth toward the olfactory bulb. Simultaneously, they maintain OP shape and position during major morphogenetic movements of the brain flexure and ensure proper tissue separation by preventing intermixing.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C142 represent the main conclusions of the study, synthesizing multiple lines of evidence. C140 is supported by observations of BM interruptions at exit/entry points (C11-C23) and axon-BM interactions (C122-C124). C141 is supported by the OP deformation and increased cell movements in mutants during flexure (C54-C64). C142 is supported by the tissue intermixing phenotype (C68-C78). These conclusions are well-supported by the collective data, though some aspects (particularly the mechanical basis of shape maintenance) remain incompletely characterized.

results.result: The authors describe the spatiotemporal dynamics of Laminin-rich basement membrane (BM) assembly around the olfactory placode (OP) and brain during early zebrafish development (17-36 hpf). They show that the OP BM assembles between 18-22 hpf during late coalescence, with contributions from OP cells, mesenchymal cells, and telencephalic cells. The BMs contain specific interruptions at exit and entry points where olfactory axons cross, and axons migrate along the brain's BM toward the olfactory bulb.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly praised the descriptive characterization of Laminin dynamics. Reviewer 1 states the authors 'describe for the first time Laminin dynamics during the early development of the olfactory placode and olfactory axon extension.' Reviewer 2 notes they 'describe the dynamic distribution of laminin γ1 in the olfactory system and forebrain' and found the results 'robust and elegant.' No concerns were raised about these descriptive findings.

results.result: In sly (laminin γ1) mutants, Laminin, Nidogen, and Collagen IV BM components are absent or severely disrupted around the OP and brain from 16-36 hpf. Electron microscopy reveals that the intercellular gap between OP and brain cells is significantly reduced (from 120 nm to 40 nm) and largely devoid of electron-dense material in mutants, while gaps within tissues are unaffected. Neural crest cells are also largely absent from the OP/brain interface.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorsed these findings. Reviewer 2 states 'They showed that in the laminin γ1 mutants no BM staining of laminin could be detected around the OP and the brain. The authors then elegantly used electron microscopy to analyse the ultrastructure of the border between the OP and the brain.' Reviewer 3 notes the study uses 'a well-established laminin-gamma-1 mutant, in which the laminin-rich basement membrane is disrupted.' No concerns were raised about the characterization of BM loss.

results.result: During OP coalescence (17-22 hpf), sly mutants show increased mediolateral dimension of the OP but normal AP and DV dimensions. Cell proliferation and apoptosis are largely unchanged. OP cell movements occur with normal mean squared displacement (MSD) and directional parameters, though brain cells show increased MSD. Overall, OP coalescence proceeds relatively normally in the absence of BMs.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes 'They show that while the OP still coalesces in the absence of Laminin, Laminin is required to contain OP cells during forebrain flexure.' This indicates acceptance that coalescence itself is not severely disrupted. Reviewer 2 states the authors 'performed a quantitative analysis of the loss of function of Laminin γ1' and found results 'robust and elegant.' No specific concerns were raised about the coalescence phenotype analysis.

results.result: During forebrain flexure (24-32 hpf), both control and sly mutant embryos show coordinated anterior-ventral movement of brain and OP cells. However, in mutants, OP cells move with higher MSD, exhibit curved trajectories, and migrate medially toward the brain rather than laterally. The authors conclude that Laminin-containing BMs are required to prevent OP cell scattering, maintain OP shape, dampen cell movements, and resist morphogenetic forces during flexure.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 explicitly states 'Laminin is required to contain OP cells during forebrain flexure during development and maintain separation of the OP and adjacent brain region.' Reviewer 2 notes 'laminin enables the shape and position of olfactory placodes to be maintained late in the face of major morphogenetic movements in the brain.' The quantitative analyses of cell movements were praised by all reviewers with no concerns raised about these findings.

results.result: At 28-36 hpf in sly mutants, the OPs are partially embedded within brain tissue with a curved, irregular boundary (versus straight in controls). The forebrain width is reduced, particularly in anterior and dorsal regions, with unchanged proliferation and only slightly increased apoptosis. The authors interpret this as tissue distortion possibly due to inward OP convergence, and conclude that BMs establish a straight brain/OP boundary preventing intermixing and late convergence.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 states the authors 'demonstrate novel requirements for Laminin in pathfinding of OP neurons towards the olfactory bulb' and 'maintain separation of the OP and adjacent brain region.' Reviewer 3 notes one caveat: 'interpretation of differences in tissue size and shape in fixed samples (comparing mutants and controls); the fixation process can alter these properties and may do so differently between genotypes.' However, this is presented as a minor caveat rather than a fundamental challenge to the findings.

results.result: Retrograde axon extension occurs in sly mutants for at least some olfactory neurons, suggesting that Laminin-dependent BMs are not absolutely required for the initial attachment of axon tips to the brain surface during this early phase of axon development.
results.evaluation: This finding is presented as part of the comprehensive analysis of axonal phenotypes. Reviewer 2 states 'Olfactory axon migration is drastically impaired in sly mutants' but does not challenge the observation that retrograde extension itself occurs. The claim is carefully qualified ('at least some neurons') and no reviewer raised concerns about this specific observation.

results.result: In sly mutants, most olfactory axons fail to leave the OP and stall at the OP/brain boundary. A small proportion (8-10%) exit dorsally (ectopically), and there are increased ectopic medial and ventral projections. Growth cones are motile but lack directional migration toward the bulb, moving short distances without preferential direction. The authors conclude that Laminin-dependent BMs are essential for axon growth and navigation from the OP to the olfactory bulb.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly endorsed these findings. Reviewer 2 states 'Olfactory axon migration is drastically impaired in sly mutants, demonstrating that Laminin γ1-dependent BMs are essential for the growth and navigation of axons from the OP to the olfactory bulb.' Reviewer 3 notes the authors 'demonstrate novel requirements for Laminin in pathfinding of OP neurons towards the olfactory bulb' and 'demonstrate that Laminin is required for growth of OP neurons from the OP-brain interface towards the olfactory bulb.' The live imaging and quantitative analyses were praised.

results.result: Neural crest cells (NCC) are absent from the brain/OP interface in sly mutants at 32 hpf, though NCC migration to the eye/OP interface is only partially impaired. The subset populating the OP/forebrain interface appears specifically affected. Analysis of foxd3 mutants (which lack NCC) shows no OP morphogenesis or axonal phenotypes, suggesting the sly phenotypes are not secondary to NCC defects.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 notes 'The authors also present data describing that while the Laminin mutant has partial defects in neural crest cell migration towards the developing OP, these NCC defects are unlikely to be the cause of the neuronal pathfinding defects upon loss of Laminin.' This indicates acceptance of both the NCC phenotype and the conclusion that it does not explain the axonal defects. No concerns were raised about this analysis.

results.result: The authors propose that the OP BM prevents deformation in response to mechanical forces from brain morphogenesis, likely through its stiffness (potentially mediated by Collagen IV rather than Laminin itself). The absence of proper BMs results in an irregular brain/OP frontier with tissue intermixing, similar to phenotypes observed in other organisms. The BMs prevent late convergence of the two OPs and maintain proper tissue boundaries.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states 'They propose that the BM of the OP prevents its deformation in response to mechanical forces generated by morphogenetic movements of the neighbouring brain.' This interpretive framework is accepted. The discussion of mechanical properties and comparison to other systems is presented as reasonable speculation. No reviewer challenged these interpretations.

results.result: The authors describe the normal trajectory of olfactory axons: after retrograde extension, axons grow using growth cones, cross the OP BM through pre-existing perforations (not by perforation), migrate dorsally between the two BMs, cross the brain BM (concomitant with axon arrival), and then grow along the internal surface of the brain's BM toward the olfactory bulb. The brain's BM serves as a migratory path.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'The authors describe for the first time Laminin dynamics during the early development of the olfactory placode and olfactory axon extension' and notes the study 'identify potential roles for Laminin in facilitating neuronal pathfinding from the olfactory placode to the brain.' The detailed description of axon trajectories relative to BMs is part of the novel descriptive findings that all reviewers praised. No concerns were raised.

results.result: The authors discuss potential mechanisms by which axons cross BMs and navigate, including possible degradation via matrix metalloproteases or displacement by protrusive forces. They propose Laminin itself as a candidate substrate for axon extension, discuss molecular mechanisms of Laminin-mediated axon growth, and consider potential interactions with guidance cues (netrins, ephrins, slits). These are presented as speculative hypotheses for future investigation.
results.evaluation: These claims are explicitly presented as speculation and discussion in the manuscript. Reviewer 3 notes the study has 'a well-written Discussion with relevance to many other systems,' indicating acceptance of the interpretive framework. The discussion is appropriately qualified and supported by citations. No reviewer challenged these speculative discussions as overreaching.

results.result: The authors conclude that the BMs of the OP and brain organize the boundary between sensory and central components of the olfactory system. These BMs are permeable at specific locations to allow axon entry, serve as substrates for axon growth toward the olfactory bulb, maintain OP shape and position during brain morphogenesis, and ensure proper tissue separation by preventing intermixing.
results.evaluation: This represents the overall synthesis of the study's findings. Reviewer 1 states the study provides 'a compelling description of the role of Laminin in olfactory placode development' and will be 'of broader interest to individuals studying extracellular matrix regulation of tissue morphogenesis, and neural development including neuronal pathfinding.' Reviewer 3 notes 'Altogether the study is extremely well carried out, with careful analysis of high-quality data.' The conclusions are well-supported by the data presented.
